title: What people do all day
intro: Ordinary actions. Most are regular; the ones whose stem changes under stress are marked irr. and given their forms.

entries.note: In much of Latin America comer on its own implies the midday meal.

ex.es: Comemos a las dos los domingos.
ex.en: We have lunch at two on Sundays.

entries.note: In Latin America tomar is the default verb for drinking, ahead of beber.

ex.en: I drink coffee in the morning.

entries.en: to live, to be alive; to reside

ex.en: What do you do for a living?

ex.es: Estudio de noche porque hay silencio.
ex.en: I study at night because it's quiet.
Write to me when you arrive.

entries.note: Deliberate listening. oír is the passive hearing that happens to you.
Directed looking, where ver is undirected seeing.

ex.en: Look at the sky, it's red.

entries.en: to look for; to pick up (a person)
entries.note: Never followed by por. Busco las llaves, not busco por las llaves.

ex.es: Paso a buscarte a las siete.
ex.en: I'll come pick you up at seven.

entries.en: to find; (encontrarse) to run into; to feel

ex.es: Me encontré con Pablo en el banco.
ex.en: I ran into Pablo at the bank.

entries.en: to think, to ponder; to intend to
entries.note: pensar en = to think about something. pensar que = to hold an opinion.

entries.en: to believe; to think (hold an opinion)

ex.es: Creo que es una buena idea.
ex.en: I think it's a good idea.

entries.en: to feel; to be sorry, to regret
entries.note: Lo siento literally means I feel it — the ordinary apology.
empezar a + infinitive. The synonym comenzar behaves identically.

ex.es: La película empieza a las nueve.

entries.en: to wait; to hope; to expect
entries.note: Three meanings English keeps apart and Spanish does not. Only context separates them.

entries.en: to ask for, to request; to order (food)

ex.en: She asked her brother for help.

ex.es: Pedimos dos tacos y una limonada.
ex.en: We ordered two tacos and a lemonade.

entries.en: to take, to grab, to catch
entries.warn: In Mexico, Argentina, Uruguay and much of Latin America this is crude slang for having sex. Neutral in Spain, where it is the ordinary word for catching a bus. Use tomar or agarrar instead and you are safe everywhere.

ex.es: En España cogen el metro; en México toman el metro.
ex.en: In Spain they take the metro; in Mexico they take the metro.

entries.note: You preguntas a question and pides a thing — the same split Hebrew makes between לשאול and לבקש.

ex.en: He asked me where you lived.
